subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: Use units as a tool to set up and check each problem. Build conversion factors that equal $1$ and orient them so the unwanted unit cancels. Track units through every multiplication and division: a correct setup leaves exactly the units the problem asks for. Give exact values where possible.

items.prompt: Convert $7$ feet to inches. Use $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.

steps: Build a conversion factor equal to $1$ that cancels feet: $\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
Multiply: $7\text{ ft}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
The feet units cancel, leaving inches: $7\times 12=84\text{ in}$.
The answer is $84$ inches.

items.prompt: Convert $48$ inches to feet. Use $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.

steps: To cancel inches, place inches in the denominator: $\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$.
Multiply: $48\text{ in}\times\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$.
Inches cancel, leaving feet: $\frac{48}{12}=4\text{ ft}$.
The answer is $4$ feet.

items.prompt: Convert $3$ minutes to seconds. Use $1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}$.

steps: Use the factor that cancels minutes: $\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}$.
Multiply: $3\text{ min}\times\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}$.
Minutes cancel, leaving seconds: $3\times 60=180\text{ s}$.
The answer is $180$ seconds.

items.prompt: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at $0$, and each gridline marks an interval of $5$ units. A bar reaches the $6$th gridline. What value does the bar show?

steps: Each gridline represents $5$ units, so multiply the gridline count by the interval.
The bar is at the $6$th gridline: $6\times 5=30$.
The bar shows a value of $30$ units.

items.prompt: Convert $2$ kilograms to grams. Use $1\text{ kg}=1000\text{ g}$.

steps: Use the factor that cancels kilograms: $\frac{1000\text{ g}}{1\text{ kg}}$.
Multiply: $2\text{ kg}\times\frac{1000\text{ g}}{1\text{ kg}}$.
Kilograms cancel, leaving grams: $2\times 1000=2000\text{ g}$.
The answer is $2000$ grams.

items.prompt: Convert $2.5$ miles to inches. Use $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.

steps: Chain two factors so miles and feet both cancel: $2.5\text{ mi}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
Miles cancel: $2.5\times 5280=13200\text{ ft}$.
Feet cancel: $13200\times 12=158400\text{ in}$.
The answer is $158400$ inches.

items.prompt: Convert $90$ minutes to hours, then to seconds. Use $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ min}$ and $1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}$. Give the answer in seconds.

steps: First convert minutes to seconds directly with the factor that cancels minutes: $90\text{ min}\times\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}$.
Minutes cancel: $90\times 60=5400\text{ s}$.
Check: $90\text{ min}=1.5\text{ hr}$, and $1.5\times 3600=5400\text{ s}$, which agrees.
The answer is $5400$ seconds.

items.prompt: A car travels at $45\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{min}}$. Use $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ min}$.

steps: Only the denominator unit (hours) changes, so multiply by $\frac{1\text{ hr}}{60\text{ min}}$ to cancel hours.
Set up: $45\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\times\frac{1\text{ hr}}{60\text{ min}}$.
Hours cancel, leaving $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{min}}$: $\frac{45}{60}=\frac{3}{4}$.
The answer is $\frac{3}{4}\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{min}}$ (that is, $0.75$ mile per minute).

items.prompt: Using distance $=$ rate $\times$ time, a runner moves at $9\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ for $4$ minutes. First convert the time to seconds, then find the distance in feet.

steps: Make the units consistent: convert $4$ minutes to seconds with $\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}$.
$4\text{ min}\times\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}=240\text{ s}$.
Substitute into $d=rt$: $d=9\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times 240\text{ s}$.
Seconds cancel, leaving feet: $9\times 240=2160\text{ ft}$.
The answer is $2160$ feet.

items.prompt: Daily high temperatures for a week range from $58^{\circ}\text{F}$ to $86^{\circ}\text{F}$. You will plot them on a vertical axis. Choose a sensible starting value (origin) and a scale (interval per gridline) so the data fills most of the axis. Give one reasonable choice and justify it briefly.
items.answer: Start the axis near $55^{\circ}\text{F}$ (not $0$) and use a scale of $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline.

steps: The data is clustered between $58^{\circ}\text{F}$ and $86^{\circ}\text{F}$, a spread of about $28^{\circ}\text{F}$.
Starting at $0$ would waste over half the axis below $58^{\circ}$, so choose an origin just below the minimum, near $55^{\circ}\text{F}$.
Pick a scale so the range fits in a handful of gridlines: $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline covers $55^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$ in $7$ gridlines.
A reasonable choice: origin at $55^{\circ}\text{F}$, scale $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline, because the data then fills most of the axis and small day-to-day differences are visible.

items.prompt: A car travels at $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$. Use $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ hr}=3600\text{ s}$.

steps: Both the numerator and denominator units change. Convert the numerator with $\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}$ and the denominator with $\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$.
Set up: $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$.
Miles and hours cancel, leaving $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$: $\frac{60\times 5280}{3600}=\frac{316800}{3600}$.
The answer is $88\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$.

items.prompt: A water tank fills at a steady rate of $4\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}$. If it fills completely in $2$ hours, how many gallons does the tank hold? Use $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ min}$.

steps: Make the units consistent by converting $2$ hours to minutes: $2\text{ hr}\times\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ hr}}=120\text{ min}$.
Volume equals rate times time: $4\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\times 120\text{ min}$.
Minutes cancel, leaving gallons: $4\times 120=480\text{ gal}$.
The answer is $480$ gallons.

items.prompt: In the formula $W=Fd$, force $F$ is measured in newtons (N) and distance $d$ in meters (m). What are the units of the work $W$? Express your answer as a product of units.

steps: Units multiply just like the quantities do, so the units of $W$ are the units of $F$ times the units of $d$.
$F$ is in newtons (N) and $d$ is in meters (m), so $W$ has units $\text{N}\times\text{m}=\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.
These combined units cannot be reduced to just N or to $\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$; the product stays as $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.
$1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ is defined as $1$ joule, so the units of $W$ are $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (joules).

items.prompt: A cyclist rides at $22\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Use $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ hr}=3600\text{ s}$.

steps: Both units change. Convert feet to miles with $\frac{1\text{ mi}}{5280\text{ ft}}$ and seconds to hours with $\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ hr}}$.
Set up: $22\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times\frac{1\text{ mi}}{5280\text{ ft}}\times\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ hr}}$.
Feet and seconds cancel, leaving $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$: $\frac{22\times 3600}{5280}=\frac{79200}{5280}$.
The answer is $15\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$.

items.prompt: A faucet drips at $\frac{1}{2}$ cup of water every $15$ seconds. Working in consistent units, how many gallons does it waste in one full day? Use $1\text{ gal}=16\text{ cups}$, $1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}$, $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ min}$, and $1\text{ day}=24\text{ hr}$.

steps: First find the drip rate in cups per second: $\frac{\frac{1}{2}\text{ cup}}{15\text{ s}}=\frac{1}{30}\ \frac{\text{cup}}{\text{s}}$.

Convert one day to seconds by chaining factors so day, hr, and min all cancel: $1\text{ day}\times\frac{24\text{ hr}}{1\text{ day}}\times\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ hr}}\times\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}=86400\text{ s}$.
Multiply rate by time to get cups per day: $\frac{1}{30}\ \frac{\text{cup}}{\text{s}}\times 86400\text{ s}=2880\text{ cups}$.
Convert cups to gallons with the factor that cancels cups: $2880\text{ cups}\times\frac{1\text{ gal}}{16\text{ cups}}=\frac{2880}{16}=180\text{ gal}$.
The faucet wastes $180$ gallons in one day.
